stances.claim: Public officials must disclose their dollar deposits in their SALNs: if not required, anti-graft laws could be easily circumvented by converting ill-gotten peso wealth to foreign currency and depositing it in banks — making SALN disclosure of dollar accounts a structural anti-corruption necessity.
stances.rhetorical_move: circumvention-prevention argument: the disclosure requirement's rationale is the ease with which its absence would be exploited

stances.claim: The House members who zealously prosecuted Corona for SALN deficiencies are hypocrites for refusing to release their own SALNs, hiding behind procedural excuses (guideline committees, review groups) when the Constitution and RA 6713 already impose a clear legal obligation.
stances.rhetorical_move: tu quoque accountability argument: those who prosecuted on SALN grounds must be held to the same standard

notable_anecdotes: HSBC's $1.9 billion settlement with US authorities for money laundering — deployed as the most vivid contemporary example of how even the world's largest banks are being held accountable for laundering illegal cash, lending urgency to the Gopac conference's money laundering agenda.

Justice Leonen appended as a congratulatory postscript — CJ notes that while Leonen gained public acclaim for the MILF peace negotiations, his 'real passion — in which he excels even more — is teaching and practicing law, and using it to champion human rights, environmental activism and indigenous people's advocacies': a personal tribute that distinguishes the public-fame reason for Leonen's appointment from the deeper legal-philosophical qualities CJ most admires.

The House members' SALN hypocrisy — forming a committee to prepare guidelines only to refer the draft to another group — as a bureaucratic stonewalling tactic CJ exposes with barely contained sarcasm, using the Corona prosecution itself as the ironic standard by which the House must now be judged.

one_paragraph_summary: Writing as a postscript to reader questions arising from the Corona impeachment dollar-deposits issue, Panganiban clarifies two points: (1) dollar deposits are perfectly legal to hold in the Philippines -- the controversy was about SALN disclosure, not legality; and (2) public officials must disclose their dollar accounts in their SALNs because if they need not, anti-graft laws could be circumvented simply by converting ill-gotten pesos to foreign currency. He notes the SC dismissed PSBank's petition as moot (impeachment trial concluded), and that the SC's opening of dollar accounts constituted a narrow exception only for impeachable officials (President, VP, SC justices, Ombudsman, ConCom members) -- private citizens' bank secrecy remains unaffected. He contextualizes the anti-bank-secrecy trend internationally: Switzerland liberalized its secrecy laws; banks must report $10,000+ transactions to anti-money laundering councils; and HSBC agreed to pay 'a whopping $1.9 billion (yes, billion)' to US authorities for a money laundering probe. He then calls out the House members who zealously prosecuted Corona on SALN grounds but refuse to release their own, hiding behind committee-to-prepare-guidelines and review-group excuses -- when both the Constitution (Art. XI Sec. 17) and RA 6713 already impose a clear SALN obligation. Appended: congratulations to newly appointed Justice Leonen (172nd SC member; UP magna cum laude; Columbia LLM; MILF peace negotiations), with CJ noting that Leonen's 'real passion -- in which he excels even more -- is teaching and practicing law, and using it to champion human rights, environmental activism and indigenous people's advocacies.'
